confirmed.title: Withdrawal tracker can mark a just-mined transfer as 'dropped' and return the funds, so the player is paid twice
confirmed.scenario: A queued test-USDT withdrawal of 1,000.00 is broadcast at nonce n. On a tracker pass, getTransactionReceipt(hash) returns 'not found' because the tx is still in the mempool, or because a load-balanced RPC node is behind. The tx is then mined in the next Arbitrum block (about 250 ms later), and getTransactionCount(from,'latest') returns n+1. track() sets the outbox row to the terminal 'dropped' status. WithdrawalBroadcasterService.track() then calls failWithdrawal(), which posts withdrawal_release (LOCKED -> AVAILABLE +1,000.00). The ERC-20 transfer is final on-chain, and the player gets 1,000.00 back in Available and can withdraw it again. Later passes never re-check, because 'dropped' short-circuits at line 209.
confirmed.evidence: chain-signer.service.ts:218-223 reads the receipt; when it is absent, lines 250-260 run `const latestNonce = await client.getTransactionCount({ address, blockTag: 'latest' }); if (latestNonce > row.nonce) { ... status: 'dropped' ... return { state: 'dropped' } }`. There is no second receipt lookup, and the nonce does not have to be consumed `confirmations` blocks deep. withdrawal-broadcaster.service.ts:213-218: any non-mined, non-pending state goes to `this.failWithdrawal(w.id, ... 'transaction dropped (nonce replaced)')`. withdrawals.service.ts:625-638 `fail()` then calls `release()`, which posts withdrawalReleaseLines (LOCKED -> AVAILABLE).
confirmed.fix: Declare 'dropped' only when the nonce was consumed at least `confirmations` blocks deep (getTransactionCount at blockTag head - confirmations + 1) and a second getTransactionReceipt(hash), made after the nonce read, still returns nothing. Otherwise return 'pending'. Do not treat 'dropped' as terminal until that check holds.

confirmed.title: Daily (KYC) withdrawal limit can be exceeded with concurrent requests
confirmed.scenario: A KYC level-1 player has a 2,000.00 daily limit and 5,000.00 Available. Two POST /withdrawals of 1,500.00 each, with different idempotency keys, are sent at the same moment. Each READ COMMITTED transaction runs the aggregate of today's withdrawals before the other has committed, sees 0.00 used, and passes. Both then reach ledger.post(), where the user_available row lock only serializes the balance check, and both succeed. 3,000.00 is locked for withdrawal on the same day, against a 2,000.00 limit.
confirmed.evidence: Lines 136-155: `const today = await tx.withdrawal.aggregate({ ... status: { in: COUNTS_TOWARDS_LIMIT } }) ... if (usedToday.plus(money(quote.amount)).gt(money(limit))) throw`. No per-user lock is taken before this check. The first per-user lock is the FOR UPDATE inside ledger.post() at line 217 (ledger.service.ts:71-75), which comes after the limit check. The idempotency row only conflicts when the key is the same.
confirmed.fix: Serialize withdrawal requests per user before reading usage. For example, run `SELECT ... FROM ledger_accounts WHERE code = 'user:<id>:available' FOR UPDATE`, or take pg_advisory_xact_lock(hash(userId)), at the top of the transaction, then aggregate today's withdrawals.

verdicts.reason:
The finding holds up in code. The daily-limit check at apps/api/src/modules/withdrawals/withdrawals.service.ts:136-155 is the only place the limit is enforced. It runs inside `prisma.tx`, which is explicitly READ COMMITTED (apps/api/src/infra/prisma/prisma.service.ts:35-40). Nothing before the aggregate takes a per-user lock:
- IdempotencyService.run (idempotency.service.ts:34-38) only conflicts on the same (scope, owner, key). Different keys insert freely.
- The userProfile read and the aggregate are plain SELECTs.
- withdrawal.create has a unique index only on (user_id, idempotency_key) and on number.
- There is no DB trigger on withdrawals, only the append-only and ledger-balance triggers in the init migration.
- No global interceptor or guard serializes per-user requests. The AuditInterceptor only applies to @Audit routes, and the ThrottlerGuard is a rate limit, not a mutex.

The first per-user lock is the FOR UPDATE on the ledger accounts inside ledger.post() (ledger.service.ts:71-76), and it is reached only after the limit check. The race then plays out like this:
1. Tx B waits on A's row lock.
2. After A commits, B's balance read is a new statement under READ COMMITTED, so it sees 5,000 - 1,500 = 3,500 available. B's 1,500 debit passes.
3. B's limit check had already passed against usedToday = 0.

Nothing later re-checks the limit:
- runRiskCheck/AML (aml.provider.ts) only flags velocity at 5 or more withdrawals in 24h, amounts of 10,000 or more, or a new destination. Two 1,500 withdrawals to a whitelisted address that has a prior confirmed withdrawal both auto-queue.
- The admin approve path does not re-check the limit either.

Step-up 2FA is not a barrier. Step-up tokens are single-use but not exclusive: a player can obtain two from POST /auth/2fa/challenge within the 5-minute TTL, or send totpCode on one request and a token on the other. This lets both requests reach the transaction at the same time.

The result is that a level-1 player (2,000.00/day) can lock and queue 3,000.00 or more in withdrawals for one day. This is a server-side limit failure, so high severity is appropriate.

The race is real. I checked every layer that could serialize the two requests or catch the overage later, and none does.

1. **Transaction isolation.** `PrismaService.tx` (apps/api/src/infra/prisma/prisma.service.ts:34-40) runs READ COMMITTED, not SERIALIZABLE.

2. **The limit check.** Inside the idempotency transaction (withdrawals.service.ts:136-155), the statements before it are:
   - an `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` into `idempotency_keys`, which only blocks when the scope, owner and key all match;
   - an unlocked `userProfile.findUnique`;
   - an unlocked `withdrawal.aggregate`.

   Two requests with different keys therefore both see `usedToday = 0`. The first per-user row lock is the `ledger_accounts ... FOR UPDATE` in `ledger.post()` (ledger.service.ts:71-75), called at withdrawals.service.ts:217. That runs after the limit check. When it unblocks, it re-reads only the balance (5,000 - 1,500 >= 1,500), so the second request passes too.

3. **Database.** The migrations have no trigger, exclusion constraint or partial unique index that enforces the limit on `withdrawals`. The only unique indexes are on `number` and `(user_id, idempotency_key)`. The only triggers are the append-only ones and the balanced-posting check.

4. **Guards and interceptors.** `WITHDRAWAL_POLICY` and `PlayerPolicyGuard` check only onboarding and restrictions. The global `AuditInterceptor` does nothing for routes without `@Audit`, and the controller writes its audit record after the commit. Nothing takes a per-user mutex or advisory lock.

5. **Step-up 2FA does not stop it.** Each request needs its own proof, but the player can get two single-use step-up tokens from POST /auth/2fa/challenge. Each takes one TOTP code: one code per 30 s step, or backup codes. A token stays valid for the configured `STEP_UP_TOKEN_TTL`, documented as 5 minutes. Both requests can then be sent at the same moment, so the 2FA gate does not stop the race.

6. **Nothing catches it afterwards.** `runRiskCheck` and the mock AML provider (aml.provider.ts:54-95) never re-check the daily KYC limit. They look only at sanctions, new destination, a velocity count of 5 or more in 24 h, amounts of 10,000 or more, and account age.

   For a whitelisted address that already has a confirmed withdrawal, the result is `approve`, the withdrawal is `queued`, and it is broadcast. The player ends up with 3,000 USDT locked or withdrawn on one day against a 2,000 limit. The server-side compliance limit is not enforced under concurrency, so severity high is appropriate.

I confirmed the finding in the code. PrismaService.tx (apps/api/src/infra/prisma/prisma.service.ts) runs every transaction at READ COMMITTED. Inside idempotency.run, the statements before the daily-limit check take no per-user lock:
1. The idempotency_keys INSERT ... ON CONFLICT only conflicts when the (scope, owner, key) triple matches, so two different keys do not block each other.
2. userProfile.findUnique is a plain read.
3. The withdrawal.aggregate at withdrawals.service.ts:136-145 is a plain snapshot read, so it cannot see the other transaction's uncommitted 'requested' row.

The first per-user lock is the FOR UPDATE on ledger_accounts inside ledger.post (ledger.service.ts:71-76), and that runs after the limit check. It serialises only the balance check. When T2 unblocks, its next statement sees T1's committed debit: 5000 - 1500 = 3500 is still at least 1500, so T2 passes too. Its stale limit check is never re-run.

Nothing else prevents it:
- No DB trigger, constraint or partial unique index on withdrawals caps the daily total. The only unique indexes are number and (user_id, idempotency_key).
- No Redis or advisory lock serialises per-user requests. The global AuditInterceptor only writes audit rows.
- ThrottlerGuard does not block two requests.

Step-up does not block the race either. Each request needs its own single-use step-up token, and a legitimate user can get two tokens one after the other (they last 5 minutes) and then fire both requests together. The limit really is level_1 = 2000.00 (packages/shared/src/limits.ts:20). Two concurrent 1500.00 requests therefore lock 3000.00 on the same day against a 2000.00 limit. The withdrawals module has no concurrency test.

I kept the severity at high: a KYC limit is not enforced on the server, though the system is demo/testnet only.

confirmed.title: RG participation limit subtracts refunds of purchases from earlier periods, so the player can stake beyond the limit
confirmed.scenario: A player has a 100.00 daily participation limit. Yesterday they bought 9 entries (90.45 USDT). That round is cancelled today, and a 90.00 'refund' transaction is created today. Today usage = Σ entry_purchase(today) − Σ refund(today) = 0 − 90.00, clamped to 0. The player can now buy entries until today's purchases minus 90.00 reach 100.00, which is about 190 USDT staked in one day under a 100.00 limit. A weekly or monthly limit is bypassed the same way when a round is cancelled at the start of the period.
confirmed.evidence: Lines 584-588: `const spent = (await this.sumOf(db, userId, 'entry_purchase', since)).minus(await this.sumOf(db, userId, 'refund', since)); if (type === 'participation') return toUSDTString(maxZero(spent));`. sumOf filters on `createdAt: { gte: since }` (line 609). Refund transactions are created at cancel time (round-lifecycle.service.ts:481-500), and nothing links them to the purchase's period.
confirmed.fix: Only net refunds whose original purchase falls in the current period. For example, sum refunds joined to entry_purchase transactions of the same round that were created since `since`, or exclude stakes of cancelled rounds by purchase date instead of subtracting refund rows by refund date.

The defect is real, but the daily example as written does not happen with the default settings.

What the code does: `usage()` at responsible-gaming.service.ts:584-588 computes participation as entry_purchase sum minus refund sum, both taken from `since = periodStart(period)`. `sumOf` (lines 603-617) filters only on `createdAt >= since` and leaves out failed, rejected and cancelled rows. `cancel()` in round-lifecycle.service.ts:481-500 creates the refund transactions with status 'pending' and createdAt set to cancel time. Pending rows are counted, and nothing ties a refund back to the period of the original purchase. The only caller is `entries.service.ts:78`, which calls `assertCanParticipate` inside the purchase transaction, and it adds no other per-period cap. A refund dated in the current period for a stake bought in an earlier period therefore lowers the current period's usage, and the player can stake the limit plus the refunded amount.

Where it is reachable:
- **Cancel paths.** `startDraw` cancels at the first tick after the 20:00 close, on the same UTC day as the purchases (`nextDailyWindow` gives 08:00-20:00 windows). `pollAndSettle` cancels for 'vrf_timeout' 24h after the draw request (`VRF_TIMEOUT_HOURS` defaults to 24), but only for non-mirrored rounds. Production forbids `RANDOMNESS_PROVIDER=mock`, so this means Chainlink without mirroring.
- **Weekly and monthly limits.** A Sunday or month-end round whose VRF is not fulfilled is refunded at about 20:00 Monday, or on the 1st. That refund cuts the new period's usage for the rest of that week or month, so the bypass described in the finding holds.
- **Daily limit, as written.** With the defaults, a vrf_timeout refund arrives around 20:00:xx on the next day. That day's round has already closed at 20:00, and the following round opens at 08:00 the day after, which is a new period. So the daily case only happens if `VRF_TIMEOUT_HOURS` is set to 11 or less, or if the BullMQ tick worker is delayed past midnight so the threshold cancel lands on the next day.

Severity: I suggest medium. The player cannot trigger it. It needs a VRF outage or a worker delay that falls on a period boundary. Once triggered, though, the RG participation and loss limits really are not enforced on the server, and the loss limit at line 590 has the same flaw.

It does work with `VRF_TIMEOUT_HOURS` set below 12 (the minimum allowed is 1): for example, a 12 h timeout cancels at 08:00 the next day, inside that day's purchase window. - In responsible-gaming.service.ts:584-588, usage() computes Σ entry_purchase − Σ refund. Both sums go through sumOf, which filters only on `createdAt >= periodStart` (line 609). Status 'pending' is not excluded, so a refund counts as soon as it is created.

- Rounds run only 08:00-20:00 UTC (nextDailyWindow, line 33). rounds.open is called only from the scheduler.
- A threshold_not_met cancel runs at the post-close sweep, so its refund lands the same day.
- A vrf_timeout cancel fires once requestedAt + VRF_TIMEOUT_HOURS (default 24, env.ts:166) has passed. requestedAt is at or after 20:00 on day N, so the refund lands at or after 20:00 on day N+1.

2. The VRF request times out, and the cancel runs on Monday after 20:00, creating a 90.00 'refund' row dated Monday. That is in the new week (periodStart uses Monday as the week start).
3. From Tuesday to Sunday, weekly usage is purchases − 90.00, so the player can stake about L + 90 in that week.

confirmed.title: Real on-chain deposits are credited to Available without the RG deposit limit, self-exclusion or deposits_blocked checks
confirmed.scenario: A player has a 500.00 weekly deposit limit, or later self-excludes, or gets a 'deposits_blocked' restriction. Their HD deposit address is already assigned. They send 5,000.00 test-USDT to it. The watcher records it (CHAIN_CLEARING -> PENDING) and after 20 confirmations credits all of it to AVAILABLE, where it can be staked. Only the DEMO simulate endpoints call assertCanDeposit, so the RG deposit limit is never enforced on the real deposit path.
confirmed.evidence: Lines 140-153 call deposits.recordDetected() and lines 246-249 call deposits.credit() with no RG or restriction check. `grep assertCanDeposit` returns only deposits.service.ts:211 and demo-deposits.service.ts:43 (both DEMO). DEPOSIT_POLICY (auth/guards.ts:41-46) only guards the HTTP address route, not the watcher. RG usage('deposit') does count these deposits (responsible-gaming.service.ts:583), so the limit is measured but never applied.
confirmed.fix: In credit(), evaluate the deposit limit, self-exclusion and deposits_blocked for the user. Post the amount that exceeds the limit, or the whole amount for blocked or excluded users, to a withdraw-only bucket (e.g. OWED or a held account) instead of AVAILABLE, and notify the user. On-chain funds cannot be refused, but they must not become stakeable.

confirmed.scenario: oddsDisclosure(35, 18640) gives firstPrizePercent '0.188' (exact 0.187768...%), and oddsDisclosure(2, 3) gives firstPrizePercent '66.667' (exact 66.666...%); I reproduced both against the built dist. confirmed.title: Deposit watcher drops a second identical Transfer to the same address in one transaction, so it is never credited
confirmed.scenario: One on-chain transaction, for example an exchange batch payout or a multisend, emits two Transfer logs of 100.00 test-USDT to the same deposit address (logIndex 3 and 5). Log 3 is recorded as DP-x. For log 5, the 'known' lookup finds DP-x (same txHash, toAddress and amount, and logIndex 3 ≠ 5), so it is treated as a moved log and skipped. The user receives 200.00 on-chain but only 100.00 is credited, and reconcile() keeps matching DP-x to log 3.
confirmed.evidence: Lines 129-139: `const known = await this.prisma.deposit.findFirst({ where: { network, txHash: log.transactionHash, toAddress: to, amount, logIndex: { not: log.logIndex ?? 0 } } }); if (known) continue;`.
confirmed.fix: Treat a log as a moved copy only when no Transfer with the recorded deposit's logIndex still exists in the current receipt, for example by matching through the receipt. Otherwise record each distinct (txHash, logIndex) as its own deposit.

Take one transaction with two Transfer logs of the same value to the same deposit address. The first log (logIndex 3) finds no row matching txHash, toAddress, amount and logIndex not 3, so it is inserted as DP-x. The second log (logIndex 5) runs the `known` lookup at lines 129-138 (same network, txHash, toAddress and amount, logIndex not 5) and finds DP-x, so `continue` at line 139 skips it. The secret check in apps/api/src/config/env.ts:33-34 is only `z.string().min(32)`, and it is used for JWT_ACCESS_SECRET and ADMIN_JWT_ACCESS_SECRET at lines 69-75. TOTP_ENCRYPTION_KEY at line 80 only gets a check that it decodes to 32 bytes. crossFieldProblems() (lines 220-248) has one production-only rule, Anvil chain 31337. Nothing in apps/api/src compares a secret to the .env.example values or to 'dev-only'/'change-me' (searched with grep). AppConfig only calls parseEnv().

The committed values pass these checks:
- .env.example:37 and :42 hold 47-50 character 'dev-only-change-me-…' strings, which clear min(32).
- .env.example:48 is a valid 32-byte base64 key.

In docker-compose.yml, the x-api anchor (lines 17-21) loads .env.example as a required env_file, with .env optional on top. The prod `api` service only overrides NODE_ENV, PRIVY_MOCK, SOCKET_IO_REDIS_ADAPTER and the shared x-api-env URLs and flags, not the secrets.

Attack (a), forged step-up token, checks out:
- step-up.service.ts:47/71 signs and verifies step-up tokens with JWT_ACCESS_SECRET (HS256, iss 'globalpool-api', aud 'step-up').
- assert() at lines 86-109 checks only typ, sub, sid, purpose and that the jti is unused.
- auth.controller.ts:74 returns sessionId to the client.
- withdrawals.service.ts:117 and security.controller.ts:95/117 accept the X-Step-Up-Token header in place of a TOTP code.
So anyone holding a player session can forge a valid step-up token and withdraw or change security settings without 2FA.

Attack (b), forged admin token, checks out:
- admin-auth.service.ts:130 writes metadata {familyId} on 'admin.login' rows.
- audit.service.ts redact() strips only password, mfaCode, totpCode, code, refreshToken and secret, so familyId is kept.
- admin.service.ts returns metadata raw (around line 430).
- authenticate() (lines 175-210) verifies with ADMIN_JWT_ACCESS_SECRET and checks typ. It then looks up a live session row by familyId and adminUserId. Rotation keeps the same familyId, so a familyId from an active admin session stays valid.
- It then loads that admin's live permissions. A forged {sub: superAdminId, sid: familyId, typ: 'admin_access'} (aud 'admin') therefore gets full Super Admin access.

The docs promise otherwise: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:130 and docs/API.md:71 say weak secrets stop the process.

One part of the scenario is overstated. Boot in production mode also needs DEPOSIT_XPUB (deposit-address.service.ts:30) and RANDOMNESS_PROVIDER=chainlink (randomness.service.ts:30), so "adds only PRIVY_APP_ID/SECRET" is not enough to start it. Neither check touches the JWT or TOTP secrets, though, so the placeholder values still reach a running production-mode API.

The compose header comment says to "set real values before any shared use". That is a warning only; nothing in the server enforces it. I keep the severity at high: this is an authentication bypass that depends on how the stack is deployed, in a DEMO/testnet build.

confirmed.title: TOTP step-up and admin-login lockout counters are stale read-modify-write: concurrent guesses bypass the 5-attempt lock and can even clear an active lock
confirmed.scenario: An attacker holds a stolen player session and sends 120 parallel wrong codes to POST /auth/2fa/challenge (the per-IP default throttle allows this). Every request loads the row while failedAttempts=0 (verifyActive: find at line 133), so every request writes failedAttempts=1 and lockedUntil=null. 120 guesses cost 1 counted failure instead of locking after 5. The lock only lands after about 5 such bursts, so roughly 600 guesses per lock window per IP versus the intended 5. A slow request still in flight (stale count 3) writes lockedUntil=null and wipes a lock that a parallel request just set. The admin login has the same pattern for password and TOTP guesses (admin-auth.service.ts:85-97).
confirmed.evidence: totp.service.ts:198-203: `const failed = row.failedAttempts + 1; … update({ data: { failedAttempts: lockedUntil ? 0 : failed, lockedUntil } })`. It uses the row read before the async verify, with no row lock or atomic increment, and writes lockedUntil=null on every non-final failure. admin-auth.service.ts:85-93: `attempts = admin.failedLoginAttempts + 1` and `lockedUntil: lock ? … : admin.lockedUntil` (the stale null overwrites a concurrent lock).
confirmed.fix: Do the increment atomically in SQL (`UPDATE … SET failed_attempts = failed_attempts + 1 … RETURNING failed_attempts`). Set locked_until in the same statement when the threshold is reached, and never write locked_until=NULL on a failed attempt. Alternatively, SELECT … FOR UPDATE inside a transaction.

verdicts.reason:
I confirmed this in code, and nothing refutes it. In totp.service.ts, verifyActive (line 133) reads the row first. verifyRow then checks the lock against that stale row (line 152), awaits otplib verify, and on a wrong code writes `failedAttempts: row.failedAttempts + 1` and `lockedUntil: null`, or a new lock, with a plain update (lines 198-203). There is no transaction, no SELECT FOR UPDATE, no atomic increment and no conditional where. Only the success path uses a conditional updateMany (lines 170-176).

Nothing else serialises these requests. POST /auth/2fa/challenge (security.controller.ts:76) has only PlayerAuth and the global ThrottlerGuard, which allows 120 requests per IP per 60 s by default (env.ts:185-186). StepUpService.challenge calls verifyActive directly, with no Redis lock or idempotency key. The only global interceptor is AuditInterceptor, which just records. The migrations have no trigger on totp_secrets; the triggers they do have are append-only guards on other tables.

So N parallel wrong codes that all read failedAttempts=k each write k+1. A request that read a lower stale count writes lockedUntil=null after a parallel request has set the lock, which wipes it.

admin-auth.service.ts has the same pattern. Line 85 computes `attempts = admin.failedLoginAttempts + 1` from the row read at line 50, and line 93 writes the stale `admin.lockedUntil` back when not locking. The window is wide there because argon2.verify runs between the read and the write. The per-IP throttle of 10 per minute (admin.controller.ts:85) reduces the burst size, but it does not close the race and using several IPs gets around it. The admin TOTP step inside login also goes through verifyRow and shares the TOTP counter race.

DEV_CONVENTIONS, API.md and ARCHITECTURE.md contain no owner decision that accepts a best-effort lockout. API.md:650 states that the account locks after ADMIN_LOGIN_MAX_ATTEMPTS.

Medium is the right severity. Exploiting the player path needs a stolen session, and brute-forcing TOTP stays slow (about 3 valid codes in 1e6), but the 5-attempt lock is clearly not enforced under concurrency.

confirmed.title: Four-eyes inbox and approval detail are gated only by dashboard.read, exposing AML holds, suspensions and flagged withdrawals to roles without users/withdrawals/aml permissions
confirmed.scenario: The Marketing Lead role has dashboard.read but no users.read, withdrawals.read or aml.read (packages/shared/src/enums.ts:469-477). They call GET /admin/approvals/inbox?view=open, then GET /admin/approvals/:id. The response contains every pending 'user.restriction.apply' request: the player's handle and publicId, the restriction type (withdrawals_frozen / account_suspended) and the compliance officer's free-text requestReason. It also contains flagged-withdrawal releases (reference, amount, withdrawal id) and the full audit trail of reasons. The equivalent list GET /admin/approvals requires withdrawals.read (admin.controller.ts:224).
confirmed.evidence: admin-console.controller.ts:51-52 and 61-62 use `@RequirePermissions('dashboard.read')` only. FourEyesService.view() returns requestReason, decisionReason and the full payload (four-eyes.service.ts:721-727). detail() adds the auditTrail with reasons (lines 256-285). inbox() never filters items by whether the viewer may see the target module. The e2e tests only exercise super_admin viewers.
confirmed.fix: Filter inbox and detail items to actions whose module permission the viewer holds (withdrawal.approve: withdrawals.read; user.restriction.apply: users.read; admin role changes: system.read). Alternatively require those permissions on the routes, and redact requestReason/payload for non-eligible viewers.

verdicts.reason:
The finding holds. Nothing in the code blocks this path.

1. **Routes.** apps/api/src/modules/admin/admin-console.controller.ts:51-52 (GET approvals/inbox) and :61-62 (GET approvals/:id) only have `@RequirePermissions('dashboard.read')`. The class-level `@AdminAuth()` only adds AdminAuthGuard (bearer token) and PermissionsGuard. PermissionsGuard (admin.guards.ts) checks the listed permissions and nothing else, and no interceptor or redaction layer is involved.

2. **Role.** The `marketing` role in packages/shared/src/enums.ts has dashboard.read, affiliates.read/manage, marketing.* and notifications.send. It has no users.read, withdrawals.read or aml.read. prisma/seed.ts seeds exactly this mapping (ROLE_PERMISSIONS), so the deployed role matches the code.

3. **Inbox.** FourEyesService.inbox() (four-eyes.service.ts:183-254) loads all pending, decided-today and expired requests with no filter on target module or permission. Each row goes through view() (:691-743). view() uses the action permission only to set `yourRole` (`not_eligible`); it never drops or redacts the row. Every row returns targetId, summary, requestReason, decisionReason and the full payload (only dedupeKey is removed).

4. **What leaks.**
   - Restriction requests: admin.service.ts:187-201 stores type (withdrawals_frozen / account_suspended), userHandle and userPublicId in the payload. The summary shows "Account suspended · @handle".
   - Flagged withdrawals: withdrawals.service.ts:397-404 stores reference WD-n and the amount.

5. **Detail.** detail() (:256-286) also returns eligibleApprovers and the audit trail with each row's reason. It makes no permission check beyond the route guard.

6. **Inconsistent with the rest of the code.** The older GET /admin/approvals list requires withdrawals.read (admin.controller.ts:223-224). The alerts endpoint under the same dashboard.read gate is filtered by role (admin-console.service.ts:864, `!a.permission || admin.permissions.includes(a.permission)`). The e2e test even treats "support has no aml.read → no-permission state" as intended (admin-console.e2e-spec.ts:417). The inbox has no equivalent filter.

7. **Docs.** docs/API.md lists these routes only as "admin" and records no decision that they should be visible to every admin.

Scenario: a marketing admin calls GET /admin/approvals/inbox?view=open, then GET /admin/approvals/:id. The responses show which players are under suspension or withdrawal holds and the compliance officer's reasons, data that role cannot get from the users, withdrawals or aml endpoints. Medium severity fits: it is a read-only information-exposure gap, and no money moves and no action can be decided (approve/reject still check the action's permission in assertDecidable).

confirmed.title: Admin 15-minute idle timeout exists only in the browser; the server refreshes an idle admin session for the full 8 h
confirmed.scenario: An admin closes the console tab, or the tab is discarded before the client idle timer runs endSession, which is what revokes the family through logout. Hours later someone at the machine uses 'Reopen closed tab' (Chrome restores sessionStorage with the refresh token), or anyone who obtained the refresh token, and calls POST /admin/auth/refresh. Refresh succeeds until the absolute ADMIN_SESSION_TTL (8 h), with no password or TOTP. On reload the web resets lastActivity to now after the refresh, so the console opens signed in even though the UI promises sign-out after 15 minutes idle.
confirmed.evidence: refresh() checks only rotatedAt, revokedAt and expiresAt (admin-auth.service.ts:136-163). No last-activity or idle check exists, and authenticate() checks none either. The idle limit is a web constant: session.tsx:29 `ADMIN_IDLE_MINUTES = 15`, enforced client-side at :204. The restore path (session.tsx:211-234) calls refresh() and then sets `lastActivity.current = Date.now()`.
confirmed.fix: Store last_seen_at on the admin session and reject refresh or access when now − last_seen_at exceeds the idle limit (15 min), revoking the family. Update last_seen_at in authenticate(), throttled.

verdicts.reason:
I confirmed this in the code. The server never enforces the admin idle limit.

- `AdminAuthService.refresh()` (admin-auth.service.ts:136-163) checks only whether the row exists and its subject, plus `rotatedAt`, `revokedAt` and `expiresAt`. `expiresAt` is set at login as now + ADMIN_SESSION_TTL, which is 8h (.env and env.ts:77). Each rotation keeps the same `expiresAt` (`row.expiresAt!` is passed to `issue()`).
- `authenticate()` (lines 175-208) checks the same fields and nothing about activity. `AdminAuthGuard` (admin.guards.ts:20-31) only calls `authenticate()`.
- There is no other guard, interceptor or DB check for admin idle time. The `Session.lastSeenAt` column exists but is never read or written on the admin paths. The 15-minute limit lives only in the browser: `ADMIN_IDLE_MINUTES` at session.tsx:29, the interval at :264-268 and the token-provider check at :204.

The failure path is reachable:
- The refresh token is kept in sessionStorage. Chrome restores sessionStorage on "Reopen closed tab", on crash or session restore, and when a Memory Saver tab that was discarded is reloaded.
- No JavaScript runs while the tab is closed or discarded, so `endSession('idle')` never fires.
- On reopen, the restore effect (session.tsx:211-234) calls `refresh()`. The server accepts it at any point within the 8h. The client then sets `lastActivity.current = Date.now()` and `signed_in`, so the console opens signed in with no password or TOTP.
- Anyone holding the refresh token can do the same by calling POST /admin/auth/refresh directly. That endpoint has only a per-IP throttle.

This makes it worse:
- Even when the client idle timer does fire, `endSession` calls `adminLogout(access.current.token)` (session.tsx:160).
- The access token lasts 15 minutes and is only refreshed on demand. After 15 minutes idle it has often already expired, so `/admin/auth/logout` (an `@AdminAuth()` route) returns 401 and the family is not revoked on the server. Only the local copy of the token is cleared.

No doc promises a server-side idle limit for admins. The behaviour still contradicts the UI and WEB_COMPONENTS.md, which promise a 15-minute idle sign-out (ADM-01). Medium severity fits, since this is a DEMO build.

confirmed.title: Admin login page redirects to an unsanitized ?next= when a session is restored (open redirect / javascript: URL in the admin origin)
confirmed.scenario: An admin tab already holds a session: its refresh token is in sessionStorage, which survives cross-origin navigation within the tab. That tab gets navigated to /admin/login?next=https://evil.example/admin/login, for example by an external page the admin opened in the same tab. The effect immediately runs router.replace(next). Next 15.5 treats a cross-origin href as external and calls location.replace, so the admin lands on a clone that asks for password + TOTP again. With next=javascript:… the same location.replace path runs script in the admin origin, which can read the refresh token from sessionStorage.
confirmed.evidence: login.tsx:244-246: `if (session.status === 'signed_in' && !previewState) router.replace(params.get('next') ?? '/admin');` has no validation. The post-login branch at :261 does check `next.startsWith('/admin')`, and other pages use safeNext(). The installed Next 15.5.29 app-router sends external URLs to `location.replace(canonicalUrl)` (node_modules/next/dist/client/components/app-router.js:84,277) and has no javascript: filter.
confirmed.fix: Apply the same check as line 261 (`safeNext(raw)` and require the '/admin' prefix) before router.replace in the already-signed-in effect.

verdicts.reason:
The finding is real. I could not refute it.

1. **The redirect is unchecked.** In apps/web/src/components/admin-a/login.tsx:244-247 the effect runs `router.replace(params.get('next') ?? '/admin')` whenever `session.status === 'signed_in'` and no preview state is active. The value is not checked. The post-login branch at :261-262 does check for the `/admin` prefix, and safe-next.ts exists, but this effect uses neither.

2. **A plain page load in the tab reaches it.** AdminSessionProvider is mounted for /admin/login by apps/web/src/app/admin/layout.tsx. On mount (session.tsx:211-247) it reads the refresh token from sessionStorage, calls refresh() and adminMe(), and sets the status to `signed_in`. sessionStorage is scoped to the tab and origin, so the token is still there when the same tab comes back to the admin origin after visiting another site.

3. **Nothing else in the path validates `next`.**
   - There is no middleware in apps/web; the only middleware files are build artifacts in .next.
   - The login page (app/admin/login/page.tsx) only wraps the component in Suspense.
   - next.config.ts sends no Content-Security-Policy, so nothing blocks a javascript: URL navigation.
   - console-gate.tsx:21 builds `next` from pathname itself, so it is safe, but that does not stop a URL the attacker writes.

4. **The installed Next does not filter the URL.** apps/web resolves to next 15.5.29. In app-router-instance.js:206-218, `dispatchNavigateAction` builds `new URL(href, location.href)` and sets `isExternalUrl` by comparing origins. A javascript: URL has origin "null", so it counts as external. navigate-reducer.js:163-164 then sends it to handleExternalUrl, which sets mpaNavigation and canonicalUrl. app-router.js:270-277 then calls `location.replace(canonicalUrl)`. The only javascript: check in next/dist/client is in form-shared.js, and it applies to form actions, not to router.replace.

5. **Impact.**
   - `next=https://evil…` sends the admin to a phishing clone.
   - `next=javascript:…` runs script in the admin origin, which can read the refresh token from sessionStorage.

6. **What limits it.**
   - It needs a live session that the refresh restores, and the admin's own tab must be navigated to the crafted URL. A new tab opened from a link (noopener) does not get the copied sessionStorage.
   - The product is DEMO/testnet only.
   - Because of these, medium is the right severity.

confirmed.title: Admin login leaks a correct password (423 instead of the generic 401) while the admin's TOTP factor is locked, and reveals existing admin emails via the 403 lock response
confirmed.scenario: An admin mistypes 5 MFA codes on console actions, which locks the TOTP row for STEP_UP_LOCK_MINUTES=15. During that window a password-guessing attacker gets 401 'Invalid email, password or authenticator code' for wrong passwords. For the right password they get 423 STEP_UP_LOCKED 'Too many incorrect codes', because verifyRow throws before the generic path, and that attempt is not counted. Separately, 5 bad attempts against a candidate email return 403 'temporarily locked' only when the account exists; unknown emails always return 401. This enumerates admin emails and lets anyone lock any admin out.
confirmed.evidence: admin-auth.service.ts:78-82 calls `this.totp.verifyRow(...)` only when passwordOk. totp.service.ts:152-156 throws STEP_UP_LOCKED (mapped to 423) when row.lockedUntil > now, bypassing the INVALID message and the failed-attempt update at admin-auth.service.ts:84-97. Lines 67-72 return a distinct FORBIDDEN error for a locked existing account.
confirmed.fix: In login, treat a locked TOTP factor as a plain failure (catch it and fall through to the generic 401 and counter update). Return the same generic 401 for locked accounts, or apply the lock uniformly by email hash.

verdicts.reason:
I confirmed both parts of the finding in the code, and nothing else in the stack prevents either one.

(1) Password oracle. In admin-auth.service.ts:76-82, verifyRow is only called when passwordOk is true. totp.service.ts:152-156 throws AppError('STEP_UP_LOCKED') before any counter bookkeeping whenever row.lockedUntil > now. ERROR_HTTP_STATUS maps STEP_UP_LOCKED to 423 (packages/shared/src/schemas/common.ts:135). That exception escapes login(), so the generic 401 INVALID path and the failedLoginAttempts update at lines 84-108 never run. A wrong password still gets 401 'Invalid email, password or authenticator code'. The right password gets 423 'Too many incorrect codes', and that attempt does not count toward ADMIN_LOGIN_MAX_ATTEMPTS. The admin's TOTP row really does get locked by ordinary use: admin-security.service.ts:38 calls totp.verifyActive({adminUserId}) for every requiresMfa console action. Five wrong codes (STEP_UP_MAX_ATTEMPTS default 5) lock it for 15 minutes. The row is the same one login reads.

(2) Email enumeration. admin-auth.service.ts:67-74 returns FORBIDDEN (403) 'temporarily locked' with lockedUntil for an existing, locked account. On the fifth failure, line 108 also returns details {locked:true}. An unknown or disabled email always gets a plain 401 (lines 51-64), and its counter never moves. This goes against the intent stated at line 52 ("Equalise timing so responses do not reveal which emails exist").

The per-IP throttle (admin.controller.ts:85, 10 per minute) only slows both attacks down. Neither docs/DEV_CONVENTIONS.md nor docs/API.md accepts this behaviour. Severity stays low: it is information disclosure and lockout denial of service, and an attacker still needs a TOTP code to log in.

confirmed.title: AML alert resolution writes its audit row outside the action, so a failed audit append leaves a resolved alert with no audit trail
confirmed.scenario: A compliance admin dismisses an AML alert. aml.resolve() commits the status change on its own (aml.service.ts:100-108). The separate audit.record() call then fails, for example on an advisory-lock or hash-chain insert error or a DB blip. The client gets a 5xx, but the alert stays 'dismissed' with resolvedByAdminId set and no audit_logs row. Architecture requires sensitive actions to write their hash-chained audit row inside the same transaction.
confirmed.evidence: admin.controller.ts:291-309: assertSensitive, then `const alert = await this.aml.resolve(id, admin.id, …)` (default db = this.prisma, no tx), then `await this.audit.record({... action: 'aml.alert.resolved' ...})` with no tx argument. AmlService.resolve accepts a `db` parameter, but the controller does not pass a transaction. resolve() also has no status guard, so resolved or auto_rejected alerts can be re-resolved.
confirmed.fix: Wrap the resolve and the audit in this.prisma.tx(), passing tx to both aml.resolve(..., tx) and audit.record(..., tx). Add a status guard (only open/under_review/escalated may be resolved).

verdicts.reason: The finding holds. In admin.controller.ts:291-306, resolveAml calls `this.aml.resolve(id, admin.id, body.resolution, body.reason)` without a transaction. In aml.service.ts:91-108 the `db` parameter then defaults to `this.prisma`, so the findUnique and update commit on their own. The controller then calls `this.audit.record({...})` with no tx. audit.service.ts:57-58 opens a fresh `this.prisma.tx(...)` when tx is undefined, so the audit append (advisory lock, read of the last hash, insert) runs in a second, independent transaction. If that second transaction throws (lock or transaction timeout, chain insert error, connection drop), the alert is already committed as resolved/dismissed/escalated with resolvedByAdminId set, there is no audit_logs row, and the client gets a 5xx. Nothing else covers the gap. The route has no @Audit decorator, so AuditInterceptor does not run for it, and that interceptor would also record outside the business transaction. The init migration has no trigger on aml_alerts. resolve() has no other caller that passes a tx. This contradicts ARCHITECTURE.md:126-127, which says sensitive actions write their hash-chained audit row inside the same transaction, and audit.service.ts:51, which says to call record(entry, tx) inside the business transaction. The side claim is also accurate: resolve() checks only that the alert exists, not its status, so an already resolved or auto_rejected alert (status 'resolved', resolution 'auto_rejected' from screenWithdrawal) can be re-resolved and its resolution text overwritten. Severity stays low: reaching the bad state needs an infrastructure failure between two commits, and the action is admin-only, behind RBAC and MFA, on a DEMO system.

confirmed.title: Compose 'prod' profile builds the web in DEV MOCK auth mode by default, so player sign-in is broken against the production API
confirmed.scenario: An operator follows the compose header: they set PRIVY_APP_ID and NEXT_PUBLIC_PRIVY_APP_ID in .env and run `docker compose --profile prod up --build`. The shared x-web build args pass NEXT_PUBLIC_PRIVY_MOCK=${NEXT_PUBLIC_PRIVY_MOCK:-true}, and .env.example also sets it to true, so publicEnv.privyMock is true even with an app id. AuthProvider mounts MockAuthProvider, which calls POST /auth/dev/token. The prod API (Privy mode) answers 404 'Cannot POST /auth/dev/token', so no player can sign in.
confirmed.evidence: docker-compose.yml:54-66 x-web args (used by both web and web-dev) with `NEXT_PUBLIC_PRIVY_MOCK: ${NEXT_PUBLIC_PRIVY_MOCK:-true}`. The Dockerfile web-build stage defaults ARG NEXT_PUBLIC_PRIVY_MOCK=true. apps/web/src/lib/env.ts:12 `privyMock: privyAppId === '' || process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_PRIVY_MOCK === 'true'`. auth-provider.tsx:21 uses MockAuthProvider when privyMock is true. auth.controller.ts:116 returns NOT_FOUND unless mode is 'mock'.
confirmed.fix: Give the prod web service its own build args with NEXT_PUBLIC_PRIVY_MOCK=false, and require a non-empty NEXT_PUBLIC_PRIVY_APP_ID there. Or make privyMock depend only on an empty app id outside development. Nothing else was left out: these 9 findings are all the defects found in this dimension.

verdicts.reason:
The finding holds. I confirmed every step in the code:
(1) docker-compose.yml:54-66. The shared x-web anchor is used by both `web-dev` (line 145) and the prod `web` (line 162). It passes build arg `NEXT_PUBLIC_PRIVY_MOCK: ${NEXT_PUBLIC_PRIVY_MOCK:-true}`, and the prod `web` service does not override it.
(2) The Dockerfile default is also `ARG NEXT_PUBLIC_PRIVY_MOCK=true` (lines 39 and 47). The value is inlined into the Next client bundle at build time, so the runtime `env_file: .env` on the web service has no effect on it.
(3) apps/web/src/lib/env.ts:12 sets `privyMock: privyAppId === '' || process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_PRIVY_MOCK === 'true'`. Setting NEXT_PUBLIC_PRIVY_APP_ID alone therefore still gives privyMock=true.
(4) apps/web/src/lib/auth/auth-provider.tsx:21 mounts MockAuthProvider, which calls authApi.devToken, i.e. POST /auth/dev/token (mock-auth-provider.tsx:170).
(5) The prod `api` service forces `PRIVY_MOCK: 'false'` and `NODE_ENV: production` (compose lines 157-158). app-config.ts:35-38 then returns 'privy' when PRIVY_APP_ID is set, or 'disabled' otherwise. auth.controller.ts:114 throws NOT_FOUND unless the mode is 'mock'.

Result: following the documented prod instructions breaks player sign-in. The compose header (lines 5-6), docs/API.md:30 and docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:167 all say only that "a Privy app id" is needed. They never mention NEXT_PUBLIC_PRIVY_MOCK=false, and .env.example:58 sets it to true, so a `cp .env.example .env` setup keeps it true too.

The only way out is for the operator to discover on their own that NEXT_PUBLIC_PRIVY_MOCK=false must go in .env, which compose uses for interpolation. Nothing in the repo tells them to do that. The failure is fail-closed (the API refuses mock tokens in production), so there is no auth bypass. It is a broken sign-in flow under a non-default profile of a DEMO-only stack, so severity stays low.

confirmed.title: Rounds already committed on-chain fall back to the DB-only draw/cancel path when POOL_ONCHAIN_MIRROR is turned off (VRF-timeout refund of an owed draw, or a mock re-roll in non-prod)
confirmed.scenario: Round #N has chainMirror=true. Its entries are committed and requestDraw has been sent to GlobalPoolRounds (on-chain status DrawRequested). The operator then restarts the API with POOL_ONCHAIN_MIRROR=false, which env validation allows. (a) With RANDOMNESS_PROVIDER=chainlink (production): if VRF is still unfulfilled after VRF_TIMEOUT_HOURS, the non-mirrored branch marks the request timed_out and cancels the round with reason 'vrf_timeout', refunding every stake to Owed. The contract never cancels a requested draw, so it later stores the VRF word and computeWinners() returns 13 winners. The DB says refunded, the on-chain attestation says drawn, and nothing ever reconciles the two. (b) With RANDOMNESS_PROVIDER=mock (any non-production env): if the round is still 'closed', startDraw creates a new mock request whose word comes from a server-generated UUID. settle() then credits winners from that word without verifyDraw. confirmed.title: Second withdrawal approval overwrites a concurrently withdrawn first approval (no status guard), releasing a flagged withdrawal
confirmed.scenario: Flagged WD-77 is under_review, and Admin A has given the first approval (pending row P). A calls POST /admin/approvals/P/withdraw to revoke it. At the same moment Admin B calls POST /admin/withdrawals/WD-77/approve. B's transaction locks the withdrawal row and reads P as pending (findFirst). A's withdraw does not lock the withdrawal row, so its updateMany(status pending -> cancelled) commits. B then runs tx.adminApproval.update({where:{id:P}}), which matches by id only and turns 'cancelled' back into 'approved'. The withdrawal moves to queued and is broadcast, although the only standing consent at execution time was B's. The audit log shows 'approval.withdrawn' followed by 'withdrawal.approve'.
confirmed.evidence: withdrawals.service.ts:388-395 reads the pending approval. Lines 428-442 check the requester, then `tx.adminApproval.update({ where: { id: pending.id }, data: { status: 'approved', ... } })` runs with no `status: 'pending'` predicate and no count check. four-eyes.service.ts:406-421 withdraw() runs its own transaction with only the approval-row CAS and never takes the withdrawal row lock that adminApprove relies on.
confirmed.fix: Claim the approval with `updateMany({ where: { id: pending.id, status: 'pending' } })` and abort with CONFLICT unless count === 1. Alternatively, have withdraw() and reject() take the same withdrawal row lock (or lock the approval row FOR UPDATE) before changing a withdrawal approval.

The finding holds. I checked each step in the code:

1. **B locks only the withdrawal row.** `adminApprove` (withdrawals.service.ts:381-442) runs in `prisma.tx`. Per infra/prisma/prisma.service.ts that is READ COMMITTED, not SERIALIZABLE. `lockRow` (line 712-717) takes `FOR UPDATE` on the withdrawals row only. The `findFirst` at 388-395 reads the pending approval P without locking it.

2. **B's write has no status guard.** It is `tx.adminApproval.update({ where: { id: pending.id } })` at 434-442: no `status: 'pending'` predicate and no count check.

3. **A's withdraw never touches the withdrawal lock.** `FourEyesService.withdraw` (four-eyes.service.ts:406-444) is reachable via POST /admin/approvals/:id/withdraw (admin-console.controller.ts:98-110). It has no action filter, so it also applies to `withdrawal.approve` requests. It only checks that the caller is the requester, then runs its own transaction with `updateMany({ id, status: 'pending' } -> 'cancelled')`.

4. **Postgres lets B's update overwrite A's cancel.** Under READ COMMITTED:
   - If A has committed, B's UPDATE sees the cancelled row. `WHERE id = P` still matches, so it writes 'approved'.
   - If A is still in flight, B waits on A's row lock, re-checks `WHERE id = P` after A commits, and overwrites the same way.
   - B then moves the withdrawal to 'queued' (`transition` checks the withdrawal status, not the approval) and enqueues the broadcast.

5. **Nothing else in the stack stops it.**
   - The init migration has no trigger or constraint on `admin_approvals` (append-only triggers cover other tables only).
   - The four-eyes inbox approve path (four-eyes.service.ts:296-301) hands off to the same `adminApprove`, so it has the same hole. Its `assertDecidable` pre-check runs outside the transaction, so it doesn't close the window.

6. **The outcome differs from the sequential one.** If A's withdraw lands first, B's call finds no pending row and only creates a new first approval, so the withdrawal stays under_review. In the race, B's single standing consent releases a flagged withdrawal. The audit log shows approval.withdrawn followed by withdrawal.approve.

Medium is the right severity: the window is narrow (a few round trips inside B's transaction) and the system is demo/testnet only.

confirmed.title: VRF event scans default to the last 50,000 blocks (about 3.5 h on Arbitrum Sepolia), so a missed DrawFulfilled leaves the round in 'drawing' forever
confirmed.scenario: POOL_CONTRACT_START_BLOCK is unset (.env.example ships it empty, and empty strings are treated as unset). VRF fulfils round #N's draw, but the rounds worker is down, or getLogs keeps failing, for more than about 3.5 h (50k blocks at roughly 0.25 s each). When polling resumes, fulfillment() scans only [head-50k, latest], finds no DrawFulfilled and returns null. In the mirrored branch, drawAttempts is not greater than known, and canReRequest() is false because the on-chain status is Fulfilled. pollAndSettle therefore returns 'waiting' on every tick and the 13 prizes are never credited, although the word is sitting in contract storage. The same window applies to request(): a DrawRequested older than the window throws RandomnessNotReadyError, and the round stays 'closed'.
confirmed.evidence: fromBlock(): `return head > 50_000n ? head - 50_000n : 0n;` when cfg.fromBlock is undefined (52-56), used by request() (60-67) and fulfillment() (93-99, `const log = logs[0]`). env.ts:150 makes POOL_CONTRACT_START_BLOCK optional, and env.ts:205 turns '' into unset. round-mirror.service.ts canReRequest() returns false unless the status is DrawRequested (516). verifyDraw already reads state.randomWord from getRound, so the value is available without logs.
confirmed.fix: Require POOL_CONTRACT_START_BLOCK when RANDOMNESS_PROVIDER=chainlink, or persist a per-round scan cursor. Better: once the contract is Fulfilled, read randomWord, fulfilledRequestId and fulfilledAt from getRound() rather than relying on a bounded log scan, and use logs only for the tx hash.

2. **A fulfilled round gets stuck in 'drawing'.** In `round-lifecycle.service.ts:pollAndSettle` (205-276), `randomness.poll` calls `fulfillment()`. confirmed.fix: Run resolve and audit.record in one prisma.tx, passing tx into AmlService.resolve (it already accepts a db argument). Guard the update with updateMany({ where: { id, status: { in: OPEN_AML } } }) and return CONFLICT when count is 0.

- The AuditService docstring says to call `record(entry, tx)` inside the business transaction.

confirmed.title: Withdrawal tracker can mark a mined transfer as 'dropped' and refund it, so the player gets paid twice
confirmed.scenario: A withdrawal tx (nonce N) is pending. The tracker calls getTransactionReceipt, which returns not-found. The tx is mined in the next Arbitrum block (about 250 ms later), or a load-balanced RPC answers the receipt call from a lagging node. The following getTransactionCount('latest') returns N+1, so track() writes status 'dropped' (a terminal state). WithdrawalBroadcasterService.track then calls failWithdrawal('transaction dropped (nonce replaced)'), which posts withdrawal_release (LOCKED -> AVAILABLE). The player has received the test-USDT on-chain AND has the full amount back in Available. They can withdraw it again.

Lines 250-260 then do: `const latestNonce = await client.getTransactionCount({..., blockTag: 'latest'}); if (latestNonce > row.nonce) { ... status: 'dropped' ... }`. The two RPC reads are not atomic, and the receipt is never re-checked after the nonce check. 'dropped' is terminal (line 209), so the row is never looked at again. withdrawal-broadcaster.service.ts:213-218 treats any non-mined, non-pending state as failure and returns the funds (withdrawals.service.ts:625-638 fail() -> release()).
confirmed.fix: Read the latest nonce BEFORE the receipt, and re-fetch the receipt after seeing nonce > row.nonce. Only declare 'dropped' once the nonce has been consumed for at least CHAIN_WRITE/WITHDRAWAL confirmations with still no receipt for our hash. For withdrawals, never auto-refund on 'dropped': park the withdrawal for manual or four-eyes review, or check that no Transfer from the hot wallet at that nonce or hash exists.

A pending tx throws TransactionReceiptNotFoundError, which is swallowed, so receipt stays null. Only after that does it call getTransactionCount('latest') (lines 250-253). If latestNonce > row.nonce, it writes the terminal status 'dropped' (lines 254-260) and never looks at the receipt again.

2. **A tx mined between the two reads is marked dropped.** If our tx is mined in that gap, the nonce is now N+1, so the row becomes 'dropped'. Line 209 then short-circuits every later track() call, so this is never corrected. A load-balanced RPC node that lags can produce the same result. The RPC client is plain viem http with no consistency guarantee (blockchain.service.ts:29).

3. **The race is reachable in normal operation.** The single worker in withdrawals.processor.ts runs with concurrency 4. It handles both WITHDRAWAL_BROADCAST jobs (one per approved withdrawal, enqueued at withdrawals.service.ts:341/483) and the repeating WITHDRAWAL_TRACK job (every 15 s). In send(), the withdrawal moves to 'broadcast' inside the outbox DB transaction (markBroadcast via onStored). That transaction commits before sendRawTransaction runs (chain-signer.service.ts:192-195). So a tracker tick that overlaps the send finds the withdrawal (status 'broadcast') and its chain row (withdrawal-broadcaster.service.ts:164-171, 198-203) while the tx is in flight. Arbitrum sequences a tx within about 250 ms, which is the same order as one RPC round trip, so the tx can easily be included between the receipt read and the nonce read. A tx whose fee is too low and sits pending across ticks gives the same window on every poll.

4. **'Dropped' leads straight to a refund.** WithdrawalBroadcasterService.track (lines 213-218) sends every state that is not pending and not mined to failWithdrawal. That calls WithdrawalsService.fail (withdrawals.service.ts:625-638), which transitions broadcast -> failed and calls release(), posting withdrawal_release (LOCKED -> Available).

5. **Nothing else catches it.** I found no reconciliation that checks the hot wallet's Transfer events or re-checks the receipt before refunding. The ledger idempotency key covers only this one event. The concurrent broadcast() may later overwrite the chain row's status from 'dropped' back to 'broadcast', because it uses the stale in-memory row.status of 'signed'. That does not undo the refund: the withdrawal is already 'failed' and is never tracked again.

**Outcome:** the test-USDT transfer is on-chain and the player also has the full amount back in Available, so they can withdraw it again.

**Severity:** this is a timing race, not something the player controls. But it will recur over many withdrawals, and each hit is a double payout from the hot wallet, so critical (money loss) fits.

2. Only after that does it read `getTransactionCount({blockTag:'latest'})`.

confirmed.evidence: chainlink-vrf.provider.ts:52-56 `return head > 50_000n ? head - 50_000n : 0n;`. Lines 92-98 call getLogs(DrawFulfilled, fromBlock, 'latest') with no chunking, unlike the deposit watcher's DEPOSIT_WATCHER_MAX_BLOCK_RANGE. round-mirror.service.ts:514-516 makes canReRequest return false unless the status is DrawRequested. round-lifecycle.service.ts:229-265 has no other exit for mirrored rounds. The contract already stores randomWord, fulfilledRequestId and fulfilledAt in getRound().
confirmed.fix: Read fulfilment from contract state (getRound: status Fulfilled, randomWord, fulfilledRequestId, fulfilledAt) rather than from logs. If logs are kept, scan in bounded chunks from a persisted cursor.

verdicts.reason:
The finding holds; I traced the failure path in code. POOL_CONTRACT_START_BLOCK is optional (env.ts:150). The env loader treats empty strings as unset, so the empty value in .env.example becomes undefined rather than 0n. crossFieldProblems (env.ts:225-234) requires an RPC, a contract and an operator key when POOL_ONCHAIN_MIRROR=true, but not a start block.

With no start block, ChainlinkVrfProvider.fromBlock() returns head-50k (chainlink-vrf.provider.ts:52-56). fulfillment() then makes one unchunked getLogs(DrawFulfilled, fromBlock, 'latest') call (lines 92-98) and returns null if nothing is found. Arbitrum Sepolia produces a block about every 250 ms, so 50k blocks is roughly 3.5 hours.

If the 30 s tick (rounds.processor.ts:26) or the RPC is down for longer than that after the contract emits DrawFulfilled (GlobalPoolRounds.sol:471), the stuck path is:
- RandomnessService.poll returns the request unchanged with status 'requested' (randomness.service.ts:78).
- In pollAndSettle's mirrored branch, drawAttempts equals the known count, so nothing new is tracked.
- canReRequest returns false because the on-chain status is Fulfilled, not DrawRequested (round-mirror.service.ts:516).
- The function returns 'waiting'. Mirrored rounds have no cancel or timeout exit (round-lifecycle.service.ts, about lines 229-265).

The round stays in 'drawing' and settle() never runs, so prizes are never credited. No other code fills the gap:
- No admin or other service writes randomWord or forces a settlement. admin-pool and admin-console only read the data.
- verifyDraw reads getRound(), but only after a fulfilled DB request already exists.
- RoundMirrorService.sync/pendingRounds does not handle drawing rounds.

The only recovery is manual: set the start block in config and restart.

The same 50k window also affects request() (lines 60-66). If the API crashes between requestDraw being confirmed and randomness.request, and stays down past the window, the round stays 'closed', because request() throws RandomnessNotReadyError on every tick.

The second half of the finding (a start block that is set makes the getLogs range grow without limit) is real in code. Whether that range gets rejected depends on the RPC provider, since the query filters on an indexed roundId and returns only a few logs. That half is plausible rather than certain.

Medium is the right severity. Settlement breaks for good, but only after an outage of several hours, and an operator can recover by changing config.

confirmed.title: The 24 h VRF re-request (contract plus automatic keeper) lets the VRF operator choose between two outcomes
confirmed.scenario: A VRF node operator, or anyone able to delay fulfilment, knows request A's output once A's block is final. If A's winners are unwanted, A is withheld. After 24 h the platform keeper automatically calls requestDraw again (request B). The operator can now compute both outputs and fulfil whichever is preferred first. The contract accepts the first fulfilment of either request. This is the 'withhold and re-request' re-roll that Chainlink's VRF security guidance warns against.
confirmed.evidence: GlobalPoolRounds.sol:407-409 allows requestDraw again from DrawRequested once 24 h have passed, and keeps the old request valid (_requestToRound is never cleared). Lines 459-471 store the first DrawFulfilled for any request of the round. round-lifecycle.service.ts:243-264 issues the re-request automatically (`this.mirror.requestDraw(round, { knownAttempts: known })`). chainlink-vrf.provider.ts:89-97 accepts whichever request fulfilled first.
confirmed.fix: Do not re-request randomness. On VRF timeout, cancel the committed round with refunds (new on-chain reason, e.g. VRF_TIMEOUT, allowed only from DrawRequested after the timeout). Alternatively, invalidate the earlier requestId when re-requesting so only the latest request can fulfil, and gate re-requests behind the admin multisig with an audit row.

verdicts.reason:
Confirmed in code; nothing elsewhere blocks it.

1. **The contract allows a re-request.** GlobalPoolRounds.sol:407-409 lets anyone call `requestDraw` again from DrawRequested once `lastRequestAt + 24h` has passed. Line 437 writes `_requestToRound[newId] = roundId` and never deletes the old mapping. `fulfillRandomWords` (lines 459-471) accepts any requestId that maps to the round while its status is DrawRequested, so the first fulfilment of either request A or request B becomes final.

2. **The contract's own tests confirm both requests stay live.** `test_ReRequest_AfterTimeout_FirstFulfilmentWins` and `test_ReRequest_NewRequestMayFulfilFirst` show that either request can win.

3. **The keeper re-requests automatically.** round-lifecycle.service.ts:243-264 calls `mirror.requestDraw(round, {knownAttempts})` when VRF_TIMEOUT_HOURS has elapsed and `canReRequest()` is true (round-mirror.service.ts:514-520 checks block time >= lastRequestAt + 24h). There is no admin gate, MFA or four-eyes approval; only an audit row is written after the fact.

4. **The provider accepts whichever request was fulfilled.** chainlink-vrf.provider.ts:89-97 takes the first DrawFulfilled log for the round. Settlement then follows that word.

**Failure path.** Only the holder of the VRF key (the Chainlink node operator) can compute a request's output; delaying fulfilment by other means, such as defunding the subscription, does not reveal it. So the actor is the node operator:
- They see A's output once its block is final and dislike the winners, so they withhold A.
- After 24 h the keeper sends B. The operator now knows both outputs and fulfils whichever they prefer.

This is a choice between two outcomes, which is worse than a plain re-roll. It is exactly the misuse Chainlink's VRF guidance warns against ("don't re-request randomness"). It also conflicts with the DEV_CONVENTIONS fairness guardrail that outcomes come only from verifiable randomness.

**Why the mitigations don't refute it.** The repo documents the risk rather than preventing it:
- packages/contracts/README.md treats it as residual risk, and its Audit TODO still says "Decide whether to keep the 24 h re-request path".
- design/figma-build/decisions.md #34 records an open product question: the design says "no re-request; auto-cancel + refunds after 24 h", while the code re-requests.
- No owner decision in DEV_CONVENTIONS accepts the re-request path.

The callback can only revert for an untrusted coordinator, and its 150k gas floor stops a fulfilment from failing by running out of gas. Neither prevents withholding.

**Severity stays medium.** Exploiting it needs a malicious VRF node operator, and the project is DEMO/testnet only.

confirmed.title: Deposit dedupe by (txHash, to, amount) silently drops legitimate transfers
confirmed.scenario: (a) One tx, e.g. a batch or multisend contract or a smart-wallet multicall, sends 50 test-USDT twice to the same deposit address (logIndex 4 and 5). The first is recorded. For the second, the 'known' query finds the first row (same txHash, to, amount, different logIndex) and skips it, so only 50 of 100 USDT is ever credited. (b) A deposit is reversed as 're-orged out' (status rejected) and its tx is re-mined later. The scan's 'known' check matches the rejected row, or createMany hits the unique key, so the re-included transfer is never credited. In both cases the funds sit at the user's deposit address uncredited.
confirmed.evidence: Lines 129-139: `const known = await this.prisma.deposit.findFirst({ where: { network, txHash, toAddress: to, amount, logIndex: { not: log.logIndex ?? 0 } } }); if (known) continue;`. There is no status filter and no per-log identity. Reversal at lines 211-212 and 298-304 sets status 'rejected' permanently.
confirmed.fix: Track each Transfer by its own identity. Match a moved log to an existing row only when that row's receipt no longer contains its old logIndex (a reconcile-owned move), and count the candidates per (txHash, to, amount) so N identical transfers create N rows. Allow a rejected (re-orged) deposit to be revived when its tx reappears in the canonical chain.

verdicts.reason:
The finding is real. I checked both scenarios against the code and found nothing else that catches them.

Scenario (a), two identical transfers in one tx:
- On the first scan the logs come back in order. Log 4 finds no row with `logIndex != 4`, so `recordDetected` creates DP for logIndex 4.
- Log 5 then runs the `known` query at deposit-chain-watcher.service.ts:129-139 (same txHash, to and amount, `logIndex: { not: 5 }`). It matches the row for logIndex 4, so it hits `continue`.
- Later scans give the same result. Log 4 ends in `createMany` with `skipDuplicates`, which returns count 0 and so null (deposits.service.ts:90-112). Log 5 keeps matching row 4. A row for logIndex 5 is never created.
- `reconcile`/`matchTransfer` (lines 261-277) only work on existing rows. For row 4 it returns 4, since that index is among the candidates. They never create rows.
- `recordDetected` is called in only two places: this watcher and the DEMO simulate paths. There is no sweep, balance check or manual-credit path that would pick up the missing transfer.
- Result: one tx that sends 2x50 test-USDT to a deposit address credits 50.

Scenario (b), a reversed deposit whose tx comes back:
- `reverse()` (lines 298-304) sets status 'rejected' for good. `reconcile` only loads status detected/confirming (line 185).
- If the same signed tx is mined again after the N-block grace period, the scan sees its log again. With the same logIndex, `known` is null, and `createMany` hits `@@unique([network, txHash, logIndex])` (schema.prisma:716) and returns null. With a new logIndex, `known` matches the rejected row, which has no status filter, and the log is skipped.
- So the re-included transfer is never credited.
- docs/API.md:521-531 and the e2e test (chain.e2e-spec.ts:541-574) only cover re-inclusion before the reversal. No test covers N same-amount transfers in one tx.

The `toUSDTString` call keeps full precision (money.ts:111-115), so this does not happen through rounding: it needs identical amounts. That is realistic for a batch, multisend or smart-wallet multicall.

Severity stays medium. Funds are left at the user's deposit address without being credited, but this is testnet/DEMO only and not exploitable for gain.

confirmed.title: A re-org that shifts log indices can collide with a sibling deposit's unique key and halt the whole watcher
confirmed.scenario: Tx T pays two platform deposit addresses: X at logIndex 7 and Y at logIndex 8. A re-org re-includes T one log later (X=8, Y=9). reconcile processes X first and runs deposit.update(logIndex: 8), which violates @@unique([network, txHash, logIndex]) held by Y. reconcile is not caught per row, so watch() returns 'skipped: reconcile failed' before scanning. The same row order repeats on every pass, so no deposit for any user is detected or credited until someone fixes the rows by hand.
confirmed.evidence: Lines 222-243 compute the new logIndex via matchTransfer and update it outside any conflict handling. Lines 84-87 abort the whole pass on any reconcile error. Rows are ordered only by blockNumber (line 190), so siblings in the same block come back in insertion order. The schema has @@unique([network, txHash, logIndex]) (schema.prisma:716).
confirmed.fix: Re-index all deposits of the same txHash together in one transaction (e.g. move them to temporary negative indices first, or process them in descending order), and catch per-deposit errors so one bad row cannot stop the watcher.

verdicts.reason:
I confirmed this in the code. In deposit-chain-watcher.service.ts, reconcile() (lines 174-258) loads open deposits ordered only by blockNumber (line 190). When matchTransfer gives a new logIndex, line 235 runs prisma.deposit.update with that index. Nothing handles a conflict there, and nothing catches errors per row. The init migration creates a plain UNIQUE INDEX on deposits(network, tx_hash, log_index) at migration.sql:1000. A unique index cannot be deferred, so the check runs at once on each update. A collision therefore throws P2002. That error leaves the loop, and watch() (lines 83-87) returns 'skipped: reconcile failed' before the scan and before the cursor upsert. The processor (deposit-watcher.processor.ts:39-41) logs this warning only once, because of the `warned` flag, so the halt is also silent after the first pass.

The scenario can happen. EVM log indices count within the block, so when a transaction is re-included at a different position, all its logs shift by the same amount. Take a tx with two qualifying Transfers to platform addresses, X at 7 and Y at 8, shifted by +1. Moving X to 8 collides with Y's row, which still holds 8. matchTransfer cannot avoid this: the only match for X is the new index 8, and it does not check for siblings. The failing update is atomic and Y is never reached, so neither row changes. Their relative order in the same block is set by the physical position of the rows or the index, and stays stable, so every later pass fails the same way. No new deposit for any user is detected or credited until someone fixes the rows by hand.

Two caveats. Whether X or Y comes first among equal blockNumbers is not guaranteed, so the halt only happens when the processing order meets the shift direction (lower row first on an upward shift, or the reverse). It also needs a re-org that moves a multi-recipient tx, which is rare on Arbitrum or testnet. That fits medium severity, not higher.

confirmed.title: Hot-wallet liquidity race: concurrent withdrawals pass the balance check and the later one fails on-chain instead of staying queued
confirmed.scenario: The hot wallet holds 100 test-USDT and two 60 USDT withdrawals are queued. The withdrawals worker runs with concurrency 4, so both WITHDRAWAL_BROADCAST jobs read balanceOf=100 and simulate transfer() at 'latest' before either tx is mined. Both are signed with nonces N and N+1. The second reverts on-chain (ERC20InsufficientBalance), and after 20 confirmations it is marked 'failed' with 'token transfer reverted on-chain'. That contradicts the documented 'missing liquidity keeps the withdrawal queued, never silently failed', makes the player redo step-up 2FA, and wastes gas.
confirmed.evidence: Lines 80-95 read balanceOf/getBalance at latest state and ignore in-flight outbox rows from the same hot wallet. Lines 96-108 send. withdrawals.processor.ts:14 sets `concurrency: 4`. Lines 213-218 fail the withdrawal on a reverted receipt.
confirmed.fix: Serialise hot-wallet sends (advisory lock), or subtract the sum of signed/broadcast-but-unmined withdrawal amounts from the balance before deciding. Treat an on-chain ERC20InsufficientBalance revert as 're-queue' rather than 'failed'. Two minor items were left out of this report: concurrent round-op step() sends across replicas, and dust deposits ignoring minDeposit.

verdicts.reason: The finding holds. In withdrawal-broadcaster.service.ts:80-95, broadcast() reads balanceOf/getBalance at the latest state and compares it only with this withdrawal's net amount. It ignores the hot wallet's own signed or broadcast outbox rows that have not been mined yet, and nothing serialises sends per hot wallet. ChainSignerService.send (chain-signer.service.ts:120-172) runs the eth_call simulation and estimateGas at latest state before taking any lock. The only lock is FOR UPDATE on the chain_signer_nonces row, and it orders nonces, not liquidity. The WITHDRAWAL_BROADCAST jobs use jobId broadcast-<id>, which is unique per withdrawal, so different withdrawals are not deduplicated. withdrawals.processor.ts:14 runs the worker with concurrency 4. The repeating trackAll job also retries queued withdrawals in the same worker, and other replicas can run at the same time. Grepping the module finds no advisory lock, unlike rounds, crash and audit. So two 60 USDT withdrawals against a 100 USDT wallet both pass the balance check and the simulation, and both get signed with nonces N and N+1. The second one reverts on-chain, and track() (lines 213-218) fails it with 'token transfer reverted on-chain' and returns the funds to Available. That contradicts the header comment (line 38) and docs/API.md:559, which say missing liquidity keeps a withdrawal queued. trackAll's sequential retry of queued withdrawals (lines 178-185) can hit the same window when the earlier tx is not yet in the latest block. Severity stays low: it is testnet only, the funds are returned rather than lost, and the cost is a needless failure, wasted gas and the player having to request again.

confirmed.title: Open redirect: safeNext() accepts '/<TAB>/host', which the browser turns into an external URL after sign-in and after the 2FA step-up
confirmed.scenario: An attacker sends a link like /2fa/challenge?purpose=withdrawal&next=/%09/evil.example/login. safeNext() lets '/\t/evil.example/login' through because the second character is a TAB, not '/' or '\'. When the player enters their TOTP code, or simply closes the dialog, StepUpPage.leave() calls window.location.assign(next). The WHATWG URL parser strips the TAB, so the target becomes //evil.example/login and the player lands on a phishing page right after proving their 2FA. The same value sent to /sign-in?next=... goes through AuthRouteOpener, which calls router.replace(next) at once for a visitor who is already signed in (no click needed). It also goes through SuccessView.proceed() (router.push(next)) after sign-in; the Next app router turns a cross-origin href into a full-page navigation.
confirmed.evidence: safe-next.ts:3 only rejects !raw.startsWith('/') || raw.startsWith('//') || raw.startsWith('/\\'). Checked with node: new URL('/\t/evil.com','http://localhost:3000').href === 'http://evil.com/', and the same happens with \n and \r\n. Sinks: components/auth/step-up.tsx:504 `const leave = () => window.location.assign(next ?? '/')`, which is called on verify (line ~539), cancel and Continue; app/(app)/2fa/challenge/page.tsx:24 passes the safeNext result straight in. components/auth/auth-route.tsx:30 `router.replace(next ?? '/')` runs for members. components/auth/auth-dialog.tsx:761 `router.push(next)`. Also onboarding.tsx:465 and two-factor-setup.tsx:224.
confirmed.fix: Reject any control character or whitespace (/[\u0000-\u001F\u007F\s\\]/) and validate with new URL(raw, location.origin).origin === location.origin, then return the url's pathname+search+hash. Prefer router.replace over window.location.assign in StepUpPage.

verdicts.reason:
I confirmed this in the code. safe-next.ts:3 only rejects values that don't start with '/' or that start with '//' or '/\'. It does not check for control characters, so '/\t/evil.example/login' passes. In the installed node, new URL('/\t/evil.example/login','http://localhost:3000').href gives 'http://evil.example/login'. That is because the WHATWG URL parser strips tab and newline characters. Browsers use the same parser for location.assign.

The path is reachable with no extra guards:
- **Step-up page:** apps/web/src/app/(app)/2fa/challenge/page.tsx:24 receives the decoded searchParams.next. There is no middleware.ts, and next.config only sets headers. The page passes safeNext's result to StepUpPage. step-up.tsx defines `leave = () => window.location.assign(next ?? '/')`. It runs on onOpenChange(false), on cancel, on Continue, and automatically in onVerified when next is set. A guest who just closes the modal is also redirected.
- **Signed-in visitor on /sign-in:** auth-route.tsx:29-30 calls router.replace(next) right away.
- **After sign-in:** auth-dialog.tsx:761 calls router.push(next).
- **Next router:** in next 15.5.29, app-router-instance.js:206 builds `new URL(addBasePath(href), location.href)` and flags it with isExternalURL. navigate-reducer.js:163 then calls handleExternalUrl, which does a full navigation to the other origin.

The existing test (test/auth.test.ts) does not cover control characters. I lowered the severity to medium because this is a client-side open redirect, useful for phishing on a demo/testnet app. It gives no script execution (the value must start with '/', so javascript: is impossible), no auth bypass and no direct path to losing money.

The finding is real. I traced every step in code and in the installed Next 15.5.29.

1. **The filter lets the value through.** safe-next.ts:3 only rejects input that does not start with '/', or that starts with '//' or '/\'. Next decodes `?next=/%09/evil.example/login` to '/\t/evil.example/login' in both server searchParams and useSearchParams (checked with URLSearchParams). That value passes the check.

2. **The URL parser turns it into an external URL.** It strips tab, LF and CR, so in node `new URL('/\t/evil.example/login', base).href` gives 'http://evil.example/login'. The same happens with \n and \r\n. Percent-encoded %09 left in the string is not stripped, so the attack depends on the decoding in step 1, which does happen.

3. **The 2FA page sink is reachable.** `app/(app)/2fa/challenge/page.tsx:24` passes safeNext() output straight to StepUpPage. In step-up.tsx, `leave = () => window.location.assign(next ?? '/')` runs on:

   - Continue;
   - AuthModal onOpenChange(false).
